title: Parsing bash, taken apart
dek: GNU bash parses with a Bison LALR(1) grammar, but only because its hand-written lexer reads and writes parser state on every word, calls the parser recursively for each $( ) and leaves every word as text for a second parser at expansion time. This teardown follows one command line from bytes to fork through bash@9c46586, then sets bash beside dash, mvdan/sh, Oils, ShellCheck, tree-sitter-bash and brush, measured on 148 tricky inputs and a 100,000-line script.
byline: 18 October 2026 · Subject: bash@9c46586 (5.3 patch 20) and five other shell parsers · Read from the source, the manual and POSIX; measured on this machine
description: How GNU bash 5.3 parses: a lexer that reads parser state, aliases, here-docs, recursive $( ), the Bison grammar, expansion, and six other shell parsers.
og_description: GNU bash read end to end at 9c46586 (5.3 patch 20): the line buffer, a lexer driven by parser state, aliases as pushed-back text, the here-doc queue, $( ) parsed three times, the 358-state Bison grammar and COMMAND tree, the parse-one-run-one loop, expansion as a second parser and arithmetic that parses data. Then dash, mvdan/sh, Oils, ShellCheck, tree-sitter-bash and brush, compared on 148 tricky inputs and a 100,000-line script.

sections.brief:
Thesis. A Bourne-family shell cannot be split into "lex the file, then parse the tokens". GNU bash keeps a Bison LALR(1) grammar anyway, and pays for it with a lexer that reads parser state, a recursive parse inside words, a second parser at expansion time and a loop that parses one line and runs it before reading the next. This section states that thesis in about 750 words, gives the reader the map, and says what they will be able to do afterwards: predict when bash parses each part of a line, read parse.y without getting lost, recognise the other five designs and their measured costs, and make the decisions a new shell parser forces.

Open on the hook, in a <pre>: for for in for; do for=for; done; echo $for prints "for" — one spelling as reserved word, loop variable, list item and assignment (G1, N69; AOSA §3.4; measured with /usr/bin/bash). Then the four breaks, one short paragraph each, each with its POSIX anchor: (1) keyword status depends on position — XCU §2.10.1 "Further distinction on TOKEN is context-dependent" and the nine rules of §2.10.2 (N94-N95); XRAT §C.2.10 defines rule 1 by "the LR(1) lookahead set" (N96). (2) here-document bodies are "a second major mode" after the next NEWLINE (XCU §2.3; N132) and "do not appear in the grammar directly" (XRAT; N133). (3) §2.3 rule 5 makes the tokenizer "recursively process" nested constructs just to find where a word ends (N426; keep the corrected wording: calling it a recursive parser is an inference). (4) the shell executes each complete_command before the next is tokenized (XCU §2.3; N117), and aliases and options such as extglob change what the lexer accepts (N51) — so parsing and running interleave.

Ramey's own account (fetched): the parser is "derived from an early version of the Posix grammar, and is, as far as I know, the only Bourne-style shell parser implemented using Yacc or Bison" and needs "a lot of cooperation between the parser and the lexical analyzer" (N1; aosabook.org/en/v1/bash.html §3.4 — keep the hedge); "Were I starting bash from scratch, I probably would have written a parser by hand" (N2; §3.7.2).

Introduce the RUNNING EXAMPLE in a <pre> and Figure {{fig-one-line}}: 18 tokens, parser_state 0 throughout, the tree (N278, N282). Say the post follows this line from bytes (§02) to fork (§09) and expansion (§10). Name the second example (trace c, here-doc plus $(case …)) in one sentence for §03/§06/§07. End with a one-paragraph map of the post: §02-§07 the lexer and what it absorbs, §08-§09 grammar, tree and loop, §10-§11 the parsers that run later, §12-§13 six other designs and the measured disagreements, §14 the decision list.

sections.title: Bytes in: the input layer and the line buffer

sections.brief:
Thesis. Before a single token exists, bash has already changed the text: history expansion has run, backslash-newline pairs have been deleted, and alias bodies may be standing in for the real input. The lexer reads only a one-line buffer, and that buffer is refilled one physical line at a time — which is where "one line is the unit" (§09) starts.

Sources and the vtable (from the code): all input goes through one global BASH_INPUT bash_input with stream types st_none, st_stdin, st_stream, st_string, st_bstream and a getter/ungetter pair (N10; bash/input.h:29, 72-84); init_yy_io installs them (N11). set_bash_input picks readline for an interactive shell with line editing, the buffered-fd reader for a non-interactive shell, stdio otherwise; bash -c never reaches it (N12; bash/shell.c:1728-1755). -c, eval, source and traps arrive as strings through parse_and_execute, which push_streams the old source (N14, N16; bash/shell.c:1483; bash/builtins/evalstring.c:340, 357).

Buffered scripts: min(file size, MAX_INPUT_BUFFER_SIZE) for seekable fds — 8192, or 8172 under bash's malloc — and one byte for an unseekable fd (N17; bash/input.c:129-133, 392). Before each fork bash seeks the fd back to the byte the parser has consumed (N18; bash/input.c:552-565; bash/jobs.c:2297-2302). Two measured oddities, shown in <pre>: printf 'read line\necho "read got: $line"\necho done\n' | bash prints only "done" (N19, G32); text appended to a running script runs, because b_fill_buffer re-reads and EOF is not sticky — not because of buffer size (N20; corrected wording; bash/input.c:488-530).

The line buffer: shell_getc serves bytes from static shell_input_line and refills only when the line is used up and no pushed string waits (N21-N22; bash/parse.y:303-309, 2498-2504). A refill reads to newline, skips NULs (N23), runs history expansion via pre_process_line (N24; 2645-2680), echoes under set -v except during a nested comsub parse (N32), and re-appends the newline (N25). Excerpt X3 (bash/parse.y:2842-2868): backslash-newline is removed here, below the tokenizer; prompt_again only selects and decodes PS2 (N26, corrected). Consequence, measured by E1 row lc02: echo a &\⏎& echo b is the operator && to bash and dash; shfmt, OSH, ShellCheck, tree-sitter and brush 0.4.0 reject, brush-parser@bd19d10 accepts; tree-sitter treats continuation as an extras token between tokens and cannot join the halves (N598, N455; tree-sitter-bash/grammar.js:103-108). Callers pass remove_quoted_newline = 0 inside single quotes (N27). A NUL byte in a script's first line makes bash refuse the file as binary, exit 126, before parsing (N33; E1 mi03 — the row that is a scoring artifact in §13).

Exceptions to "the lexer sees only the line buffer": here-doc bodies read raw via read_a_line -> yy_getc, and time_command_acceptable peeking (N21, corrected). Running example: one shell_getc call reads the whole line while the parser is in state 0, parser_state 0x0 (gap-e2e-trace F8; lab/results/trace-a.txt).

Figure {{fig-input-layer}}. Excerpt budget: 1 (X3). Badges: from the code, measured here (G32, lc02 from lab/scripts/run_e1.py -> lab/results/e1-matrix.md). Owned elsewhere: push_string and the synthetic space (§05), read_a_line for bodies (§06), PS2 printing from inside shell_getc while yyparse is suspended (§09).

sections.brief:
Thesis. bash's lexer is pulled one token at a time from inside yyparse, and each decision it makes depends on state that it and the grammar actions both write. State flows in both directions; the grammar is small because this channel exists.

yylex (excerpt X1, bash/parse.y:3055-3094, trim the mailbox comment): prompts if interactive at a command boundary, shifts the three-token history (two_tokens_ago <- token_before_that <- last_read_token <- current_token), calls read_token(READ) (N34). push_token shifts too; its only caller is builtins/evalfile.c:333, a fake newline after a sourced file ending at EOF; parse_compound_assignment reads without shifting (N35, corrected). token_to_read is a one-token injection slot read first: '\n' after an error or after time, COND_END after [[ … ]], and the synthetic DOLPAREN/DOLBRACE that start nested parses (N36; X2 parse.y:3570-3579 may be quoted inline in two lines). Operators are hand-coded if/switch with one or two characters of lookahead (<<-, <<<, &>>, ;;&); other_token_alist exists only to name tokens in error messages (N38). Character classes come from the generated sh_syntaxtab; metacharacters ()<>;&| (N37). # begins a comment only at token start (N42; echo a#b #c prints a#b).

The three stores: token history; counters — open_brace_count, esacs_needed_count, expecting_in_token, and the 256-deep compoundcmd_lineno stack, used only to say "unexpected end of file from `while' command on line N" (N78); parser_state, one int of 28 PST_* flags, five marked unused (N79; bash/parser.h:29-56). Writers: the lexer sets PST_CASEPAT on ;; ;& ;;& (N39; you may show X4 instead of X1 if the budget is tight, not both), PST_SUBSHELL on (, PST_ALLOWOPNBRC on ) after WORD ( (N40); keyword matches set PST_CASESTMT / PST_CONDCMD (N65, detail §04); grammar helpers write back — make_simple_command sets PST_REDIRLIST at a fresh command and clears it at the first word (N83; bash/make_cmd.c:480-490), actions pop compoundcmd_top (N224) and inject tokens. The set/clear sites are 74 grep hits, only in parse.y and make_cmd.c (N80). bash's own DEBUG dump_pflags tests 27 of the 28 (N85). reset_parser zeroes everything on error, frees the line and plants token_to_read = '\n' (N81). Ramey: the parser "has to tell it something about how far it has progressed parsing a command" (N84, AOSA §3.4). Mention the 11 of 16 dead LEX_* flags left by the pre-2021 comsub scanner in one sentence (N56).

Measured: the running example never sets a bit (parser_state 0x0 for all 18 tokens, trace-a.txt) — simple commands need only the token history. Trace (c) shows the flips (Figure {{fig-pst-strip}}): inside $(case x in x) echo y;; esac), CASE gives 0x4080c0, IN adds PST_CASEPAT (0x4080c1), the pattern's ) clears it, ;; sets it again, ESAC clears both (N144, DOSSIER §1.3).

Run-time globals: @( becomes an extglob pattern only if extended_glob is on when the word is lexed (N51; X10 parse.y:5464-5466 as a 3-line quote); shopt -s extglob; echo @(a|b) on one line is a syntax error, two lines work, and bash -n rejects even the two-line form because -n never runs shopt (N596; G17-G18; lab/results/tricky.txt).

Figure {{fig-feedback-loop}} carries the two-way picture. Excerpt budget: 1 (X1 or X4). Badges: from the code, measured here (trace-a.txt, trace-c.txt, bash runs). Owned elsewhere: the classification order and reserved_word_acceptable (§04), [[ ]] and (( )) as lexer-side sub-parsers (§08), DOLPAREN's nested parse (§07).

sections.brief:
Thesis. The grammar sees WORD, ASSIGNMENT_WORD, NUMBER, REDIR_WORD and 22 keyword tokens, but which one a word becomes is decided in C at the end of read_token_word, in a fixed order, each step implementing a POSIX rule the yacc listing hands back to the lexer. A keyword is a word in command position, nothing more.

The order (excerpt X7, bash/parse.y:5742-5772): special cases; reserved words in posix mode; alias expansion if unquoted; reserved words in default mode (N102). Figure {{fig-classify}} draws it.

NUMBER (POSIX IO_NUMBER): all digits, and the character that ended it is < or >, or the previous token was <& or >& (N61; parse.y:5727-5740; the comment says "&" but the code tests LESS_AND/GREATER_AND — code wins). Measured, in a <pre>: echo 2>/dev/null x; echo 2 >/dev/null; echo a2>/dev/null; echo end prints x and end (N62, G12). Running example: 2 is NUMBER(284) value 2 (trace-a.txt).

special_case_tokens (parse.y:3339-3489): in as the third word after for/case/select (rule 6), do after for x or for ((…)), esac right after in, { after a function header, } with an open brace, -p after time, ]] inside [[ (N70). The in of case sets PST_CASEPAT, so case if in if) echo matched-if;; esac works (N71, G9). esac is not a keyword after | or ( ("phantom rule 4", 2/19/2021), and esac right after in is always ESAC, so case esac in esac) is an error — POSIX applies rule 4 to the first pattern word only, so bash is right and brush wrong (N72-N73, G10-G11).

Reserved words: CHECK_FOR_RESERVED_WORD matches only an unquoted, $-free word where reserved_word_acceptable(last_read_token) holds — the lexer's oracle for command position, whose default: branch reads globals — and it mutates state (PST_CASESTMT, PST_CONDCMD, counters) (N65-N66; X6 cited). ARITH_CMD and COND_END joined that list on 2/16/2021 (N67). word_token_alist: POSIX's 16 plus select, function, time, [[, ]], coproc = 22 (N64, N98). Measured (N68): echo if then fi } prints the words; { echo a } is incomplete; >/dev/null if true; then echo x; fi fails (G2, G3, G6). time is a keyword only after specific tokens and, in posix mode, not before -p (N74); echo hi | time runs a command named time (N75).

Assignments: quote "This is context-dependent, so it cannot be handled in the grammar" (parse.y:5784-5786; N86). assignment() finds = or += after a valid name (N87). W_ASSIGNMENT anywhere; W_NOSPLIT, hence ASSIGNMENT_WORD, only in assignment position — LC_ALL=C has flags 0x14 (gap-e2e-trace F11). Declaration builtins, eval and let set PST_ASSIGNOK: declare a=(1 2 3) works, echo b=(1) is a syntax error, command declare c=(7 8) works only in posix mode (N88-N89, G14-G15). {fd} before < or > is REDIR_WORD, POSIX 2024's optional IO_LOCATION; exec {fd}>/dev/null; echo fd=$fd prints fd=10 (N63, N428, G13).

sections.title: Aliases are text pushed back into the lexer
figures: fig-alias-push · SVG · a frame stack over time for the input line s ll x with alias s='sudo_ ', alias sudo_='echo SUDO ', alias ll='echo LL': columns = steps (read word s -> push 'sudo_ ' -> read sudo_ -> push 'echo SUDO ' -> read echo, SUDO -> end of text: synthetic space, pop, AL_EXPANDNEXT -> PST_ALEXPNEXT -> ll expanded -> push 'echo LL' -> pop -> x); rows = pushed_string_list frames above the real shell_input_line; token output along the bottom: echo SUDO echo LL x. Side panel: why alias hi=…; hi on one line misses — one inputunit is lexed and parsed before anything runs, so the alias table changes after the hi token was already read · data: N103-N110, G34-G36; bash/parse.y:2018-2076, 2783-2840, 3249-3282; bash/alias.c:141-146
sections.brief:
Thesis. bash expands an alias by pushing its value back into the lexer's input and lexing it again as if it were source text. That is why an alias can contain half an if, an unclosed quote or a lone {, why an alias defined on a line does not apply on that line, and why no other parser reproduces bash's behaviour exactly.

Ramey: "The bash parser implements aliasing completely in the lexical phase, though the parser has to inform the analyzer when alias expansion is permitted" (N101; AOSA §3.4).

Mechanism (from the code): alias_expand_token fires in command position or when PST_ALEXPNEXT is set, skips an alias marked AL_BEINGEXPANDED, and returns RE_READ_TOKEN after push_string (N103; excerpt X13, bash/parse.y:3249-3276). push_string saves the current line on pushed_string_list and makes the alias text the line (N104; 2018-2076). When the text runs out, shell_getc returns one synthetic space (PST_ENDALIAS) and then pops (N105; parse.y:2783-2840) — POSIX §2.3.1's "may behave as if an additional <space>". A value ending in a blank sets AL_EXPANDNEXT, which pop_string turns into PST_ALEXPNEXT (N106; bash/alias.c:141-146; parse.y:2096-2099). command_token_position counts PST_REDIRLIST as command position, so aliases expand after a leading redirection but never on a redirect target (N82). The alias_expand() in alias.c is readline's alias-expand-line, not the parser (N115).

Measured (each in a <pre>, run with shopt -s expand_aliases where needed): same-line definition gives "hi: command not found", 127; next line works (N107, N109, G34-G35); s ll x prints SUDO echo LL x (G36); alias q="echo \"open" then q close" prints open close (G37); alias begin="if true; then" then begin echo inside; fi prints inside (G38) — every parser's -n rejects it (E1 al03, N595); alias LEFT="{" then LEFT echo one; echo two; } prints one, two, while OSH exits 2 and ShellCheck reports SC1089 (N108, G39, N572). An alias in a function body binds at definition (N110, G42). In default mode an alias is checked before reserved words, so alias if=echo then if hello prints hello; posix-mode bash and dash keep the keyword (N114, G43). eval "alias e3=…; e3" fails the same way (N118, G45). One sentence on $( ): default mode defers alias expansion to the child, posix mode expands during the read-time parse (N111-N112, G41) — details in §07.

POSIX framing (from the docs): 2024 leaves aliasing reserved words unspecified (Issue 7 forbade it in grammatical context) and allows the trailing-space chain (N116); alias changes take effect no later than the end of the current complete_command (N117); bashref says aliases expand "when a command is read" (bash/doc/bashref.texi:8580-8588), which §07 shows is incomplete.

Contrast in one paragraph, no excerpts: OSH expands after parsing a simple command by building a string and parsing it with a new parser — the one runtime->parser channel — and cannot do { or for…do aliases (N541); mvdan expands word-level in its interpreter and rejects values containing ; (N497); brush expands at run time, "a total hack" (#57) (N515); ShellCheck does not expand but warns SC2262 for same-unit use (N570); tree-sitter has none (N473).

Figure {{fig-alias-push}}. Excerpt budget: 1 (X13; X14 the synthetic space may replace it). Badges: from the code, from the docs, measured here. Owned elsewhere: comsub alias timing (§07), alias policy advice (§14), OSH internals (§12).

sections.title: Here-documents: a queue drained at the newline
figures: fig-heredoc-timeline · SVG, wide · trace (c)'s three input lines as a line buffer across the top (line 1 'cat <<A; echo $(case x in x) echo y;; esac)', line 2 body, line 3 'A'); beneath, a timeline of events: LESS_LESS WORD reduced by rule 26 -> push_heredoc, need_here_doc=1 (no body read); ';' ; nested comsub parse for $( ) (need_here_doc saved/0 inside); outer '\n' about to be returned by read_token -> gather_here_documents reads lines 2-3 raw via read_secondary_line/read_a_line; line counter 1 -> 3; then the '\n' token reaches yyparse. Thick black = control order, thin blue = bytes, dashed purple = need_here_doc/redir_stack state. Inset box: the EOF) back-compat branch in make_here_document (line starting with the delimiter and containing ')' ends the body, rest pushed back by shell_ungets, full_line = 0 -> misleading 'delimited by end-of-file' warning) · data: N119-N131, N290; X15-X18; lab/results/trace-c.txt
sections.brief:
Thesis. Here-document bodies are not tokens and not grammar. bash queues the redirect when the grammar reduces << WORD and reads the bodies raw, in order, when the lexer is about to hand the parser the next unquoted newline. Every working implementation converged on that FIFO; the edge cases are where they diverge.

Mechanism (from the code): only << and <<- call push_heredoc, not here-strings (N119; parse.y:622-681); trace (c) shows rule 26 reduce and need_here_doc go to 1 with no body read (N290). redir_stack holds at most HEREDOC_MAX = 16; the 17th is a fatal syntax error, exit 2, "maximum here-document count exceeded" (N120, G57; X15 cited). gather_here_documents drains in order (N121; X16 cited). Callers: read_token just before returning an unquoted '\n' (excerpt X17, parse.y:3646-3651), and simple_list/compound_list actions and parse_command as backstops. Measured (resolves C7): "LAB HEREDOC gather_here_documents need_here_doc=1 line=1" comes right before the outer '\n' token and the line counter jumps 1 -> 3 (N122; quote both trace lines in a <pre>).

Bodies: read_secondary_line sets PS2, read_a_line reads yy_getc, bypassing the line buffer (N123). Any quoting in the delimiter disables expansion; E"N"D counts as quoted (N124, N126). <<- strips leading tabs only; the terminator must match exactly and be followed by a newline, so EOFX and EOF plus two spaces are body text (N125, N127, G49-G50). Running to EOF is a warning (make_cmd.c:626-627), which POSIX allows: "should, but need not, treat this as a redirection error" (N128; XCU §2.7.4). POSIX calls bodies a second "major mode" after the next NEWLINE (N132).

The compat branch (excerpt X18, bash/make_cmd.c:605-611): inside $( ), a line that starts with the delimiter and contains the closing ) ends the body; the rest is pushed back with shell_ungets, its only user (N29). full_line = 0 is set first, so 5.3 prints "delimited by end-of-file". CHANGES for 5.1 says this is no longer allowed (CHANGES:1812-1813); the code still accepts it — deprecated, not removed (N129, C4). Measured: x=$(cat <<EOF⏎hi⏎EOF) gives the warning and [hi] (G54). Bodies pending when a comsub's inner parse ends are read from the outer input after "command substitution: 1 unterminated here-document" (N131, G56).

Convergence (one paragraph): mvdan drains a FIFO when its lexer emits a newline (N490); OSH fills a pending list at the next Op_Newline word after Chu retracted a 2016 tree walk — "In retrospect, this is the obvious algorithm.  I was being too clever." (N537; oilshell.org/blog/2017/11/28.html); ShellCheck reads bodies inside its linefeed combinator (N558); brush reorders tokens so each body follows its tag (N509); tree-sitter keeps a stack in its external scanner, ends on a prefix match, and heredoc_redirect swallows the rest of the line, so two here-docs on one line have no derivation (N460-N465; E1 hd02/hd03). Divergence, measured: EOF plus two spaces — bash body text, OSH ends there and runs EOF as a command, ShellCheck SC1118 ends there, brush rejects (N560); unterminated — bash warns, dash silent, the rest reject (N585).

Figure {{fig-heredoc-timeline}}. Excerpt budget: 2 (X17, X18). Badges: from the code, from the docs, measured here (trace-c.txt, E1 rows, bash runs). Owned elsewhere: tree-sitter incremental reparse (§13), FIFO advice (§14), saving the here-doc stack around $( ) (§07).

sections.title: Command substitution: a recursive yyparse that keeps only text
figures: fig-three-parses · SVG, wide · three swim lanes for echo $(case x in x) echo y;; esac): (1) READ TIME, inside the outer yylex: parse_comsub checks $((, save_parser_state, flags PST_CMDSUBST|PST_EOFTOKEN|PST_NOEXPAND (0x408040), shell_eof_token=')', current_token='\n', token_to_read=DOLPAREN, nested yyparse from state 0 (shift DOLPAREN -> state 28) while the outer stack 0 56 139 13 is frozen; print_comsub; tree disposed; the word stores the re-print. (2) EXPANSION in the parent: extract_command_subst -> xparse_dolparen -> parse_string with DOLPAREN injected, parser_state 0x8040 (no NOEXPAND), rewind_input_string finds the end, tree discarded (a cm_case). (3) CHILD after fork: command_substitute -> remove_quoted_escapes -> parse_and_execute(…, "command substitution", pflags|SEVAL_NOHIST) in another pid. Mark alias policy per lane (lane 1 only in posix mode; lane 2 expand_aliases=0; lane 3 re-enabled outside posix mode) and the exceptions as notes: $(( textual, inside an unquoted here-doc body not parsed at read time, $(<file) can skip lane 3, ${ cmd; } runs lane 3 in-process, backquotes skip lane 1 · data: N136-N158, N336, N341, N343; X19-X24; lab/results/trace-c.txt
sections.brief:
Thesis. Since bash 5.2 a $( ) is parsed by calling the real parser recursively from inside the lexer; the tree is thrown away and only its pretty-printed text is kept as the word. That text is parsed again at expansion to find where it ends, and a third time in the forked child. Backquotes never got this treatment.

History (from the docs): CWRU/changelog, 6/19/2021: "rewrite to recursively call the parser (yyparse()) and return a string constructed from the resulting parse tree. Probably will only work with bison" (N136; changelog:1386-1394; shipped in 5.2, 2022-09-26). Since 4.0 bash had parsed $( ) to find its close (N161). AOSA's description predates the rewrite (N4).

Read time: parse_comsub first checks $(( and, per POSIX interp 217, collects a matched pair (N138). Otherwise excerpt X19 (parse.y:4499-4549, trimmed to ≤25 lines; say what was cut): save_parser_state (flags, token history, here-doc and alias stacks, even $?) (N140); set PST_CMDSUBST|PST_EOFTOKEN|PST_NOEXPAND, shell_eof_token = ')', current_token = '\n', token_to_read = DOLPAREN "let's trick the parser", r = yyparse () (N139). Hand-saving is needed because Bison's stacks are yyparse locals but yychar and yylval are globals (N141). The grammar reaches comsub: DOLPAREN compound_list ')' via an alternative of inputunit (N142); yylex never produces DOLPAREN (N143). Measured: the outer stack 0 56 139 13 waits at "Reading a token"; the nested parse starts at state 0, parser_state=0x408040, and shifts DOLPAREN into state 28 (N144).

Text, not tree: excerpt X20 (parse.y:4626-4646): print_comsub re-prints; a leading space if the text starts with ( so it cannot become $(( (N145). Measured with declare -f: comments and spacing in $( ) vanish, backquote bodies stay verbatim — show the f(){ echo $(echo a   ;   echo b) "${ echo c;}" `echo   d`; } example and output in a <pre> (N146).

Three parses (N151, C5): (1) parse_comsub at read time; (2) xparse_dolparen, called from extract_command_subst at expansion: injects DOLPAREN, runs parse_string with expand_aliases = 0, learns the end through rewind_input_string ("need to do more validation on xchars value for sanity -- test cases."), discards the tree; measured parser_state 0x8040, no NOEXPAND (N153-N155); (3) parse_and_execute in the child (N336; subst.c:7376-7413). Trace (c) shows all three, the second a discarded cm_case, the third in another pid (N152). Exceptions: inside an unquoted here-doc body no read-time parse; $(( and SX_COMPLETE extraction is textual (N156); $(<file) can skip the child (§10); ${ cmd; } runs in-process (N163).

Consequences, measured: a syntax error in $( ) is caught at read time, even by bash -n, and nothing on the line runs (N150, G66); backquotes are scanned by parse_matched_pair, so `for` passes bash -n and fails in the child (N58, G65; textual since 3.2, N162); aliases in $( ) expand at read time only in posix mode, otherwise in the child (N111-N112, G41). The $(( fallback: param_expand jumps to comsub when chk_arithsub fails (N157); echo $((echo hi); (echo there)) passes bash -n and prints hi there, dash says Missing '))' (N158, G72), as POSIX §2.6.3 requires (N159).

Figure {{fig-three-parses}}. Excerpt budget: 2 (X19, X20). Badges: from the code, from the docs, measured here (trace-c.txt, declare -f runs). Owned elsewhere: exit status of a failed comsub parse (§09), read_comsub and CTLESC (§10), dash and OSH keeping the inner tree (§12).

sections.title: The Bison grammar and the COMMAND tree
figures: fig-precedence · SVG, wide · left: the nonterminal ladder inputunit -> simple_list -> simple_list1 -> pipeline_command -> pipeline -> command -> {simple_command, shell_command (11 alternatives), function_def, coproc} with the three precedence lines (%left '&' ';' '\n' yacc_EOF; %left AND_AND OR_OR; %right '|' BAR_AND) drawn as bands beside the levels they settle; right: a table of tree shapes, each a small binary tree: a; b; c left-heavy; a | b | c right-nested; a && b | c with && above | (the running example, decided by the reduction of rule 173 in state 237); a; b & c after connect_async_list moves & onto the last ; element; [[ a || b || c ]] right-nested via the lexer's recursive descent · data: N183-N194, N208, N214; X27, X31, X38; lab/build/e3/parse.output; trace-a.txt

fig-command-union · SVG, wide · struct diagram with the running example's tree as the instance: COMMAND {type, flags, line, redirects, value} with line shown as 0xdfdfdfdf (never set); value -> CONNECTION {ignore, first, second, connector} for && and |; SIMPLE_COM {flags, line, words, redirects}; words -> WORD_LIST -> WORD_DESC {word 'LC_ALL=C', flags 0x14}, {sort}, {-u}; redirects -> REDIRECT {redirector 0, r_input_direction, 'in.txt'}, {redirector 2, r_output_direction, flags 0x241, '/dev/null'}; callouts: make_command's type pun through value.Simple, lists built backwards and reversed once by clean_simple_command, |& desugared to a 2>&1 REDIRECT, ! and time as CMD_* flag bits · data: N225-N240, N199, N196, N282; X37; trace-a.txt
sections.brief:
Thesis. With context work done in the lexer, the Bison grammar is small and has no unresolved conflicts; precedence declarations, not one nonterminal per level, decide the shape of lists and pipelines; the tree is a C tagged union whose words are still unparsed text. A printer turns any tree back into text and shows what the tree dropped.

Tables: y.tab.c is Bison 3.8.2 output: YYNTOKENS 63, YYNNTS 40, YYNRULES 180 with $accept, YYNSTATES 358 (N167-N168). parse.y has 48 names on %token lines, 49 with yacc_EOF; 63 = 3 specials + 49 + 11 literals (N169, C3). Measured (lab/scripts/e3_bison.sh -> e3-bison.txt): bison 3.8.2 regenerates y.tab.c in 0.53 s with 0 differing non-#line lines, no unresolved conflicts, 45 shift/reduce conflicts resolved by %left/%right (N174) — so NEWS 2.0's "all 66 shift-reduce conflicts are gone" means unresolved ones (N175, C1).

Precedence (excerpt X27, parse.y:428-432): %left '&' ';' '\n' yacc_EOF; %left AND_AND OR_OR; %right '|' BAR_AND (N183). List rules such as list1 AND_AND newline_list list1 are ambiguous binary recursions settled by those lines, so lists are left-heavy (N184); pipelines are right-nested and execute_pipeline walks ->second (N185). Running example, measured: a command-initial WORD enters state 13, holding both simple_command_element: WORD • and function_def: WORD • '(' ')' …, so one more token is read before reducing (N201; X36 from lab/build/e3/parse.output, 4 lines); on lookahead AND_AND in state 237 rule 173 reduces the pipeline first, putting && above | (N186); 19 shifts, 43 reductions, deepest stack 7 (N279); rule 1 ends the parse with YYACCEPT, $end never shifted (N281). POSIX spends a nonterminal per level and splits cmd_prefix/cmd_suffix; bash lets any element appear anywhere (N200, N430-N432).

Fix-ups: connect_async_list rotates & onto the last ; element, since yacc groups a; b & as (a; b) & — sleep 0.5; echo A & echo B keeps sleep in the foreground, ~537 ms (N193-N194); ! toggles with XOR so ! ! cancels (N196); |& becomes a 2>&1 redirect (N199). Outside the grammar: [[ … ]] is a recursive descent inside read_token that hands Bison one COND_CMD token — "we slip a mini recursive-descent parser in here" (N213); ((…)) is one ARITH_CMD only if its matching ) is followed by ), else its text is pushed back as nested subshells: ((echo a); echo b) runs two (N217, G74).

The tree: COMMAND {type, flags, line, redirects, value}, 15 command types (N225-N226). Excerpt X37 (bash/make_cmd.c:164-174): make_command stores every payload through value.Simple and zeroes its first int, a type pun, and never sets COMMAND.line; the trace sees malloc's 0xdf scramble, line = -538976289 (N229-N230; whether anything reads it is open). CONNECTION is binary, so a pipeline is not its own node type (N227-N228). SIMPLE_COM holds one flat WORD_LIST of assignments, name and arguments plus REDIRECTs; WORD_DESC is {char *word; int flags} (N231-N233). Lists are built backwards and reversed once — "It seems simpler to do this here the one time" (N240).

Printer: elif becomes else if, |& becomes 2>&1 |, redirections move after words, comments vanish, ! time -p prints time -p ! (N243, N245); idempotent on all 118 printable corpus inputs (N246; e3_roundtrip.py).

Figures {{fig-precedence}} and {{fig-command-union}}. Excerpt budget: 2 (X27, X37). Badges: from the code, from the docs, measured here. Owned elsewhere: one-line units and error recovery (§09), [[ ]] evaluation (§11).

sections.title: One unit at a time: reading, running, failing
figures: fig-reader-loop · SVG, wide · left half: the cycle reader_loop -> read_command -> parse_command -> yyparse -> global_command -> execute_command -> dispose_command -> repeat, drawn over a 4-line script (echo line1 / echo line2 / if then / echo line4) with a column marking which lines ran (line1, line2 yes; error at line 3; line4 never read), and the -n variant (execute replaced by dispose). Right half: the longjmp map for bash -c 'echo $(for)': parse_comsub (nested parse fails) -> jump_to_top_level(FORCE_EOF) -> parse_and_execute catches, unwinds, rethrows -> run_one_command: case FORCE_EOF: last_command_exit_value = 127; versus the script path where reader_loop keeps 2; below it the measured matrix rows (echo $(for) -c 127 / file 2; for) 2 / 2; : ${x?unset} 127 / 1; $((1+)) 1 / 1). Thick black = control, dashed purple = longjmp · data: N247-N254, N260, N268-N274; X40-X44; lab/results/trace-exit127-matrix.txt
sections.brief:
Thesis. bash never holds a tree for a whole script. reader_loop parses one inputunit — one line, extended only as far as an open construct needs — executes it, disposes it and reads on. That explains why earlier lines run before a later syntax error is found, why PS2 is printed from inside the lexer, why an error drops a whole line, and the 127 that bash -c returns for a broken $( ).

The loop (from the code): reader_loop sets a setjmp target, read_command -> parse_command -> yyparse, takes global_command, executes, disposes, loops (N247-N248; bash/eval.c:61-211). simple_list admits no significant newline, so a top-level unit is one line; && and || may be followed by a newline, ; and & not (N190). bash -n is the same loop with dispose in place of execute (N251; excerpt X40, bash/eval.c:147-153). bash -c runs ONESHOT main -> run_one_command -> parse_and_execute, the same alternation over a string (N254).

Measured: a script with a syntax error on line 3 prints line1 and line2 first (N249, G86); bash -c 'echo a; fi; echo b' prints only the error (N250, G85). POSIX requires the incremental model and XRAT defends it with self-extracting archives (N446). brush, by contrast, refuses the whole file (N584; §12).

The running example executes (trace-a.txt): execute_command_internal's switch -> execute_connection(&&), left side via execute_command with CMD_IGNORE_RETURN (N284) -> execute_connection('|') -> execute_pipeline, one pipe per element, fds 4 and 3 (N285) -> execute_simple_command forks before expand_words "so assignment statements [do not affect] the parent shell's environment" (N286; quote bash/execute_cmd.c:4524-4529) -> the child sets CMD_NO_FORK and execs in place, cmdflags 0x48 (N287); echo done runs as a builtin in the parent (N283). Child pids 263855 and 263856, parent 263854.

PS2 is a lexer side effect: after for i in 1 2⏎ the LR stack is 0 4 66 151 218 255 295 318 — state 318 is for_command: … list_terminator newline_list • DO compound_list DONE — when print_prompt is called from inside shell_getc (N255-N257; lab/results/trace-interactive.txt via lab/scripts/trace/pty_interactive.py, --noediting). The parser never returned.

Errors: yyerror calls reset_parser, which plants a newline so error '\n' matches; that rule accepts only at an interactive top level (N260, N189). Status EX_BADUSAGE 2, or EX_BADSYNTAX 257 inside a builtin running parse_and_execute (N265).

The 127 (measured; lab/scripts/trace/exit127.sh -> trace-exit127-matrix.txt, identical on three binaries; N268): bash -c 'echo $(for)' exits 127; bash -c 'for)' and the same text as a file exit 2; : ${x?unset} gives 127 under -c and 1 from a file; $((1+)) gives 1. Cause (N269): parse_comsub's failed nested parse calls jump_to_top_level(FORCE_EOF); each parse_and_execute level rethrows; run_one_command maps any FORCE_EOF to a literal 127 — excerpt X42 (bash/shell.c:1457-1483, trimmed to the switch) — while reader_loop keeps the 2. run_wordexp maps the same way (N270); a plain -c syntax error never longjmps (N271). The docs promise only "non-zero" (N274). Whether the mapping is deliberate is open (DOSSIER §11 Q2): do not call it a bug.

sections.title: Expansion is a second parser
figures: fig-ctlesc · SVG, wide · a byte strip for the traced word "$x"*'a b'$(echo c) with x=X, one row per stage: source word as stored by the lexer (quotes and $ intact) -> after expand_word_internal: ^A X * ^A a ^A ␠ ^A b c (CTLESC cells in orange, raw cells in white; the unquoted * and the comsub output 'c' raw) -> after IFS splitting (unchanged, one field; a quoted space cannot separate) -> glob pattern handed to glob_filename: X*a bc (CTLESC turned into a backslash only before glob-special characters, so none remain here) -> argv <Xa bc>. Above the strip, the stage order in code with the sub-parser each stage calls: brace expansion (brace_gobbler -> extract_command_subst -> xparse_dolparen) -> one left-to-right scan: tilde, param_expand / parameter_brace_expand, expr.c, command_substitute, process substitution -> word_split (only if something expanded and W_NOSPLIT clear) -> glob_expand_word_list / dequote_string -> leading assignments last · data: N291-N362; X47-X51; lab/results/ctlesc-trace.txt (lab/scripts/ctlesc_trace.sh); ^A = CTLESC \001, ^? = CTLNUL \177
sections.brief:
Thesis. yyparse stops at words: a WORD_DESC reaches the executor spelled as in the source. subst.c parses each word again, character by character, at every execution — a second tokenizer with its own matchers for ${ } and $( ) — and carries quoting through splitting and globbing as in-band marker bytes. Quote removal is a function that strips them.

Where and in what order (from the code): execute_simple_command calls expand_words at each execution (N291). Order in code: copy; separate leading assignments; brace expansion; one pass of tilde, parameter, arithmetic, command and process substitution, then splitting; glob or dequote; assignments last (N293; bash/subst.c:13219-13279). Compare the manual and POSIX, which has no brace step and puts quote removal last (N297). AOSA: "a small pipeline unto themselves" (N298). Running example: expand_words takes [LC_ALL=C][sort][-u] and returns [sort][-u]; the assignment goes to the temporary environment (N288, N294).

The second tokenizer: expand_word_internal is a switch on each character — CTLESC, < >, [, =, :, ~, $, backquote, backslash, quotes — returning 0, 1 or many words (N310). ${ } operators are parsed only here; extract_dollar_brace_string is a third } matcher beside the lexer's (N300, N327). Brace expansion runs first and is "strictly textual" per bash.1:3444-3450, yet brace_gobbler calls extract_command_subst and so the yacc parser to skip a $( ) — code wins (N322); {a,$(echo x,y)} gives a x,y and n=3; echo {1..$n} gives {1..3} (N321, N323).

The encoding: CTLESC \001 marks a protected character, CTLNUL \177 a quoted empty string (N302-N304); the lexer escapes literal \001/\177 so data cannot pose as markers (N53). Measured with the ctlesc build: "$x"*'a b'$(echo c) with x=X becomes ^AX*^Aa^A ^Abc (N362, G115). Splitting needs something expanded and W_NOSPLIT clear (N296); string_extract_verbatim skips each CTLESC with its character, so a quoted space never separates (N351; X47 cited). IFS=:; x=a::b gives 3 fields, the empty one a CTLNUL word with flags 0x40002 (N353, G116). lib/glob knows nothing about CTLESC (N358); excerpt X49 (bash/pathexp.c:244-270, ≤25 lines): quote_string_for_globbing turns CTLESC into a backslash only before glob-special characters (N357), so the pattern is X*a bc and argv Xa bc. Quote removal is dequote_string, inside glob_expand_word_list or dequote_list (N360). Results are never re-tokenized: x="echo hi; echo there"; $x prints hi; echo there (N318, G122).

Comsub output: read_comsub reads 4096-byte chunks, drops NULs with one warning, and CTLESC-quotes every byte in double quotes but only marker bytes otherwise, so unquoted output still splits and globs (N346). $(<file) parses the text to a COMMAND, checks its shape with can_optimize_cat_file and reads the file in the parent: x=$(<f$((n++)).txt) leaves n=1 (N343-N345, G82). ${ cmd; } runs in the current shell; its assignments persist (N341-N342).

Contrast, two sentences: mvdan's Word is a list of 9 WordPart kinds, so expansion walks a tree (N493); OSH parses ${…} into a typed BracedVarSub (N333); brush keeps words as strings for a second PEG (N514).

sections.brief:
Thesis. Several bash parsers run on run-time strings, not on the script: expr.c parses and evaluates arithmetic in one pass, parses variable values as expressions, and lets a subscript inside such a value trigger full word expansion — which is how data becomes code. eval, source, traps, comsub children and function import share one parse-one-run-one loop; Shellshock was that loop run on environment text.

Arithmetic (from the code): expr.c is recursive descent, one C function per precedence level from expcomma to exp0, over intmax_t; no tree; skipped operands are parsed under a noeval counter that suppresses assignment, lookup and division by zero (N363-N364): echo $(( 0 && 1/0 )) prints 0. echo $(( 2 ** 3 ** 2 )) $(( -2 ** 2 )) prints 512 4 (N365, G135). Excerpt X54 (bash/expr.c:1227-1241): expr_streval parses a variable's value with subexpr, recursion capped at 1024 (N366-N368, G133). c='$(echo 3)'; echo $(( c )) is a syntax error — the value is not word-expanded (G134) — but a subscript inside it is: array_expand_index runs expand_arith_string, full word expansion (N369; bash/arrayfunc.c:1366-1376).

Injection (measured): with x='a[$(echo PWNED >&2)]', $((x)), (( x == 0 )), [[ $x -eq 0 ]], let y=x, a declare -i assignment, [[ -v $x ]], printf -v "$x", read "$x" and ${!x} all run the command; unset "$x" no longer does (N370, G129). The 5.2 defence covers only subscripts written in the expression: $(( a[$k] )) with k='$(echo PWNED >&2)' is a syntax error at compat 53 and runs at BASH_COMPAT=51 (N371, G132). shopt -s array_expand_once needs EXP_EXPANDED, which at the default level only let passes: it stops let, not $((x)) (N372, G130); the manual says more (bash.1:11843-11851) — code wins (N373). test "$x" -eq 0 demands an integer and runs nothing (N377, G131). Put these in a small <table> (construct | runs the command?), measured cells only. OSH refuses command substitution in dynamic arithmetic; brush refuses to parse the value (N376).

[[ ]] at run time: cond_expand_word never splits, dequotes the left side, and passes the right side of ==/=~ through quote_string_for_globbing so quoted parts are literal; extglob is forced on (N379-N382). x="a*"; [[ abc == $x ]] matches, [[ abc == "$x" ]] does not; set -x shows [[ a* == a\** ]] (N383, G127-G128).

One loop for strings: parse_and_execute parses one command, runs it, repeats; -c, eval, source, traps, PROMPT_COMMAND, comsub and function import differ only in SEVAL_* flags (N386-N389). So eval "alias e3=…; e3" misses (N118) and a trap string is parsed only when it fires (N393, G137).

Shellshock: before 2014 the importer pasted "name " onto any value starting "() {" and called parse_and_execute(…, SEVAL_NONINT|SEVAL_NOHIST), so code after the body ran (N398; ftp.gnu.org/gnu/bash/bash-4.3-patches/bash43-025). bash43-025 added SEVAL_FUNCDEF|SEVAL_ONECMD, bash43-027 the BASH_FUNC_name%% names, bash43-030 the parser_remaining_input test (N398-N399). Today, excerpt X58 (bash/builtins/evalstring.c:465-475): reject unless cm_function_def, empty parser_remaining_input(), unchanged name (N396-N397). Measured on 5.3.9: env 'x=() { :;}; echo VULN' bash -c 'echo probe-done' prints only probe-done (N400, G138-G139). The exported value is bash's re-printed body, so the importer parses printer output (N401). POSIX refused exported functions over this risk (N403); export -f still exists (N404).

Figure {{fig-data-to-code}}. Excerpt budget: 2 (X54, X58). Badges: from the code, from the docs (patches, manual, XRAT), measured here. Owned elsewhere: -c and the 127 (§09), CTLESC (§10).

sections.brief:
Thesis. Every shell parser answers two questions — who owns the lexer's context, and when each sub-language (comsub, arithmetic, ${ }, here-doc bodies, aliases) is parsed — and the answers predict its measured behaviour (§13). Figure {{fig-technique-map}} places them. About 130-170 words per implementation: mechanism first, one measured consequence each.

Lineage (≈150 words): Thompson's V6 shell tokenized a whole line, then parsed — the last clean split; if and goto were external programs (N405-N406; Research-V6:usr/source/s2/sh.c:152-163). Bourne's V7 sh (version string 1978-11-06) is recursive descent in C dressed as ALGOL 68 by mac.h; term() does reserv++ and word() consults the keyword table only while reserv is set (N409-N414; X61 cited); comsubst() parsed backquotes during expansion (N415). Duff: "nobody really knows what the Bourne shell's grammar is", the routines "all have a flag argument that subtly changes their operation" (N417; omit the year). KornShell gave $( ), (( )), [[ ]] and ;& (N421-N424); POSIX.2 published the first grammar in 1992 (N425).

dash: one C function per level (list, andor, pipeline, command, simplecmd); the parser sets a three-bit checkkwd (CHKALIAS|CHKKWD|CHKNL) before each readtoken(), keyword before alias; $( ) is parsed by a recursive list(2) at lex time and its tree kept (N442-N444; master 49f04dd). Measured: 0.054 s per 100k lines, flat 1.7-2.5 MiB; accepts 101 of 148, rejecting bash extensions (N577, N580, N601).

mvdan/sh: streaming, non-backtracking recursive descent over an io.Reader in 1 KiB chunks (N478); the parser sets p.quote to one of 21 single-bit quoteStates and preNested/postNested save it (N480; excerpt X67, sh/syntax/parser.go:681-741, trimmed to ≤25 lines); keywords are _LitWords checked only at statement start (N482); "$(( and (( ambiguity is not supported" because "Backtracking would complicate the parser and make streaming support via io.Reader impossible" (N486; sh/README.md:71-78).

Oils/OSH: excerpt X83 (oils/frontend/lexer.py:336-363) — the mode is a parameter of Read and the lexer stores none (N523); each mode is a regex list compiled by re2c into one DFA (N526); 22 modes + Undefined under a stale "Fifteen" comment (N525); a hint stack rewrites the next ) (N528); $( ) is a new CommandParser on the same lexer, no text copied (N534); text is re-parsed in exactly four places (N546); Pratt arithmetic (N544); lossless tree (N545); one logical line at a time except -n (N543). Figure {{fig-osh-modes}}.

ShellCheck: one 3,673-line Parsec module, scannerless (N554-N555); here-docs read by the linefeed combinator (N558); ambiguity by backtracking, then SC1102/SC1105 notes (N562); undecidable a[k] re-parsed after the fact by looking for declare -A anywhere in the file (N565); a real failure yields no AST (N567).

tree-sitter-bash: 1,201-line grammar.js -> 350,631-line parser.c, 7,571 states; lexing only for tokens valid in the state; a 1,217-line external scanner with a valid_symbols mask (N448-N456); its heredoc stack must serialize into ≤1,024 bytes each time the scanner recognises a token (N459); GLR recovery never fails and accepts invalid input (N457, N474).

brush: a grammar-blind tokenizer emits Operator/Word tokens and reorders here-doc bodies; a peg 0.8.6 grammar mirroring POSIX §2.10 backtracks — (( tries arithmetic, then subshell (N501-N509; X78 cited); words, arithmetic and comsub bodies stay strings until expansion (N514); whole-file parsing forces extglob on and run-time aliases, "a total hack" (N515).

Excerpt budget: 2 (X67, X83). Badges: from the code, from the docs (READMEs, dated blog posts, Duff), measured here. Owned elsewhere: the measured matrix and charts (§13), advice (§14).

sections.brief:
Thesis. On 148 tricky inputs the parsers disagree exactly where a parser must decide when to parse: late textual parsing makes bash -n accept what static parsers reject, a lexer that reads run-time state makes bash -n reject what runs, and here-docs are the largest single source of divergence. Speed and memory follow the architecture: parse-one-run-one stays flat, whole-file trees grow linearly, a linter pays two orders of magnitude.

E1 method (lab/corpus/make_corpus.py -> lab/scripts/run_e1.py -> lab/results/e1-matrix.csv, e1-summary.txt): accept = rc 0 for bash/dash/brush/osh -n and shfmt -ln bash; ShellCheck rejects on any SC1000-1999 at error level; tree-sitter on any ERROR or MISSING node; env -i, 10 s timeout, one run; bash-exec is a three-state reference. One bit per parser — two parsers can accept and build different trees (N614). Stat tiles (.measured): 148 inputs · 79 unanimous (71 accept, 8 reject) · 8 genuine bash -n vs run disagreements · 123 accepted by bash -n.

Results: every all-reject input is a context-free token error (N579). Accepts: bash 123, dash 101, shfmt 119 (pin 121), tree-sitter 110, OSH 117, ShellCheck 116, brush 121 (pin 123); bash-exec runs 126 (N577). Disagreements with bash -n: dash 30, tree-sitter 29, ShellCheck 21, shfmt 20 (pin 18), OSH 20, brush 18 (pin 16), bash 5.3.9 0 (N578). bash -n vs run: 9 scored, 8 genuine, mi03 an artifact (N253).

Themes, each pointing to its section: late parsing — (( 1 + )) and $(( 1 + )) pass bash -n, dash and brush, fail statically elsewhere (N583); ${x y} (N591); eval 'if' (N597). Run-time lexing — alias-to-if (N595), extglob from the previous line (N596). Here-docs — unterminated (N585), EOF) in $( ) (N586), 16 vs 17 (N587), <<$X (N588). (( — ((echo a); echo b) is two subshells to bash, dash, OSH, brush, an error to shfmt, ShellCheck, tree-sitter (N582). Lexical — &\⏎& (N598), trailing backslash (N599), CRLF (N600). Version skew: shfmt release vs pin, brush release vs pin (N491, N521). Note POSIX "need not"/unspecified cases only where the dossier states them (N128, N160, N116). Figure {{fig-disagreement}}.

E2 (lab/corpus/make_e2.sh; lab/scripts/run_e2.py, run_e2_rss.py; 1 warm-up + 5 runs, medians): 100k-line medians as in the figure (N601); dash 3.5x faster than bash (0.1863 / 0.0537; N604); startup-corrected lines/s on bash's 24,753-line configure: dash 1.52 M, bash 746 k, shfmt 375 k, OSH 194 k, brush 190 k, tree-sitter 60 k, ShellCheck 1.3 k (N603). Memory: bash and dash stay flat because each command is disposed (§09); whole-file parsers grow ≈2.5 (brush), 1.5 (OSH), 1.1 (tree-sitter), 0.8 (shfmt), 19 (ShellCheck) KiB per line (N605-N606); ShellCheck ≈654x slower and ≈386x the memory of bash -n, as a linter (N609). Caption caveats: shfmt includes printing; brush and OSH include interpreter startup; spread up to 2x; release builds for shfmt and brush; RSS floor (N610-N611).

E4 (lab/scripts/e4_incremental.py, median of 7): on a 4,992-line file with 192 here-docs a one-byte edit reparses in ~2 ms (≈48x faster than ~97 ms full); breaking a delimiter costs 16-23 ms and invalidates to EOF; tree-sitter then keeps 101 of 192 bodies while bash swallows to EOF and fails on the unclosed { (N612-N613). Figure {{fig-speed-memory}}.

No code excerpt. Badges: measured here, lab caveat once; reconstruction for the sentences linking numbers to architecture. Owned elsewhere: mechanisms (§02-§11), the decision list (§14).

sections.brief:
Thesis. The implementations amount to a decision list, and each decision has a measured cost. This section turns the post into advice for someone writing a shell parser — for a formatter, linter, editor or a shell that executes — without new mechanism. Every recommendation cites the section and the E1 row or code fact behind it.

Structure: one framing paragraph (what you build decides most answers: an executor must match bash's late parsing, a tool wants typed trees), Figure {{fig-decision-table}}, then one paragraph per decision (8 × ~90 words):

(1) Decide when each sub-language is parsed. Eager typed trees (OSH, mvdan, tree-sitter) catch $(( 1 + )) statically but must refuse or guess at $((echo a); (echo b)); bash's late handling is POSIX-conforming there and lets bash -n miss errors (N583, N158-N159; §07, §13). (2) Decide who owns lexer context and make it explicit — a mode argument (OSH), a parser-set field (mvdan), a valid-symbol mask (tree-sitter) or ordered choice (brush, ShellCheck) rather than shared globals; bash's author would hand-write the parser today (N2, N523, N480). Badge as reconstruction. (3) Model here-docs as a FIFO drained at the next newline token; every working implementation converged on it, Oils after retracting a tree walk, and a one-node design cannot hold two bodies on one line (N537, N465; §06). (4) Handle ((/$(( with bounded lookahead or backtracking, or document refusing, as mvdan's README does (N486, N505, N533). (5) Choose an alias policy: compatibility needs text push-back inside the lexer (N104); everyone else approximates and lists failures (N515, N541; §05). (6) If you execute, parse one complete command at a time: POSIX requires it (N117), memory stays flat (N605), and whole-file parsing forces workarounds like brush's always-on extglob (N515). (7) Keep source positions and a printer: idempotence tests and an X-ray of what the AST drops (N245-N246; OSH's lossless tree N545). (8) Test differentially against real bash: brush runs 3,209 YAML cases with bash as oracle, 718 known_failure (N517); mvdan checks parses against bash 5.3, dash, mksh R59 and zsh 5.9 (N496); OSH's spec suite has 223 files, 3,968 cases, and at least one BUG-bash annotation is stale for 5.3.9 (N550). Close with Ramey: "I would have introduced something like formal bash compatibility levels earlier" (N6, AOSA §3.7.2), tied to BASH_COMPAT changing parser behaviour (N440, N165, N371).

Optional, ≤20 lines: pseudocode in <pre>, badged reconstruction and labelled as from no implementation, of a recursive-descent command parser calling next_token(mode) and draining a pending_heredocs list when a newline token arrives. Generic names; no claim it compiles.

Then a short "test inputs to start with" <pre> drawn only from the gallery with bash's measured output as trailing comments: G1, G12, G24, G35, G46, G54, G72, G74, G85, G129. Escape every <, >, &.
